articles.full_text:
Sweltering summer temperatures look set to spur the earliest Champagne harvest on record and potentially one of the most challenging. The French region's winemakers face lower crop yields, weaker consumer demand and a threat to the iconic drink's famed fresh taste.
The Champagne season officially starts on Aug. 15 this year, with the majority of picking expected between Aug. 20 and 25, around two weeks earlier than usual in recent years. Before the early 2000s, harvesting the grapes of the sparkling wine — which brought in $6.6 billion in sales revenues last year — almost always took place in September or October.
But hotter springs and summers are accelerating the grape-ripening process, creating more sugary fruit and narrowing the optimum picking window for Champagne.
Winemakers are torn between harvesting early to reduce the amount of sugar in the fruit, but risking the ability to achieve the correct balance of acidity and so-called "phenolic ripeness," the point when tannins and other compounds have matured enough to deliver the desired flavor and texture.
"With great wine grapes, you want the maturation process to be slow. This is true with most fruit," said Linda Johnson-Bell, founder of the Wine & Climate Change Institute consultancy.
A short growing window can be more easily disguised in red wines, many of which have increased their alcohol content in recent years due to more sugary grapes. But it is a particular challenge in Champagne, where the drink's "identity is its tautness, its high acidity, low sugar, its finesse, its elegance," Johnson-Bell said.
Along with a warming trend pushing harvesting seasons earlier, European wine growers are up against drought, freak weather events such as spring hailstorms and frost which wiped out many buds, and wildfires.
In the macro picture they also face waning demand for alcoholic drinks, higher labor and fuel costs, and the complication of tariffs in the U.S., Champagne's largest export market.
Some winemakers are reacting by pulling out vineyards, changing their grape varieties, moving further north or introducing irrigation systems. But high-end variants such as Champagne are restricted by their appellation, which protects where its grapes can be grown and how, including a ban on the watering of adult vines.
Champagne growers are developing various techniques to protect grape clusters, a representative from trade association Comité Champagne told CNBC. Those include the use of insect-proof greenhouses and experimenting with new grape varieties, along with the creation of an R&D center to explore further solutions.
Producers have also trimmed their quota of yield permitted for sale this year, a decision made to help balance stocks, maintain quality and preserve vineyards amid "challenging" weather conditions and "sluggish" French demand, the Comité Champagne said in a release last month.
The businesses which sell their end product will be little-concerned by this year's harvest since the "quality seems promising, and the industry could do with lower inventory," Bernstein's global head of luxury goods, Luca Solca, said by email.
Jean-Claude Mas, founder of Domaines Paul Mas-Coté Mas, which produces reds, whites and rosés in the southern French region of Languedoc, said his vineyards had so far defied gloomy expectations since he began harvesting earlier this month and were looking "beautiful."
"In 30 years I've never seen a year like this. We've had an accumulation of heat since the end of May. I was so stressed, but this year it looks like we could have a really good harvest. My analysis of that is just the incredible capacity to adjust of nature," he said.
The earlier grape harvesting season is also being observed in the U.K., which has a relatively small but growing wine industry that produced roughly 16.5 million bottles last year and increased its exports by 55%, according to official data.
"It's quite astonishing how far forward the harvesting has come in a generation," Fergus Elias, director of wine at Balfour Winery, said from a vineyard in Suffolk, England. As a child, he recalls his winemaker father's harvests never starting before early October and finishing as late as mid-November.
"If I really wanted to, I could pick these vines and make a passable wine with them," he said this week.
"But in England our growing season is still long enough... I'm quite excited," he added.
A warmer climate is allowing new varieties of grape to grow in Britain's chalky soil, which is similar to that of northern France. The opportunity has even attracted the attention of French producers, with Champagne house Taittinger acquiring land in Kent to make an English sparkling wine.
"Climate change is talked about as something that makes English wine more sustainable, although it does come with a lot of challenges," Elias said. "This year we had a late spring frost in mid-May, but we're lucky to have sites across the country which gives some geographic security."
Industry players are meanwhile convinced that Champagne's innovation will be enough to preserve the drink's status and quality long into the future.
"The Champenois will do absolutely everything to safeguard that product, they've been onto these issues for decades," Linda Johnson-Bell said. "Maybe I'm romantic but I just see Champagne always surviving."

Heatwave brings boost for tourism across region
Tourism businesses across the South West and Channel Islands have reported higher visitor numbers during the summer's heatwaves.
Atlantic Reach holiday park and Cornwall Slip and Slide, near Newquay, have reported a 10% increase which the team has attributed to the heatwaves.
In Devon, trustees at the outdoor, charity-run Victoria Pool said the heat had resulted in more swimmers and lower costs, since the sun had warmed the water and reduced the need for gas boilers.
A restaurant owner in Jersey said his business had experienced the strongest summer in its 25-year history, while Visit Guernsey has reported a 5% rise in June's accommodation occupancy rate compared to June 2025.
In Buckfastleigh, Devon, the heatwave has delivered a different kind of financial benefit.
The team at Victoria Pool, a charity-run outdoor swimming pool, said soaring temperatures had significantly reduced the heating costs while attracting record numbers of swimmers.
Trustee James Rice said the weather had created a "double whammy" for the organisation.
"The heat has helped us so much with the cost of heating the pool," he said.
The pool is normally heated by two gas boilers, but Rice said the recent sunshine meant they had barely been needed.
"I don't think our boilers have had to work," he said.
"The sun has pretty much done the job for us for, I think, the last 10 weeks."
He said the heat has also helped bring more visitors through the gates.
Rice said the opening weeks of the season were potentially the busiest since the pool reopened under community ownership more than a decade ago.
A business owner in Jersey has said although the heatwaves had led to some closure, they had also attracted more customers.
Ian Carr, owner of the Waffle House in St Helier, said he had been forced to close during the hottest days of the year because equipment and staff had struggled to cope with the conditions.
"We did have to close for the three hottest days which has never happened in the 25 years that I've been doing this," he said.
Despite that setback, Carr said the summer had been one of the strongest he could remember.
He said fewer rainy days had helped increase turnover and attract more customers, including growing numbers of visitors from France, Germany and the Netherlands.
However, Carr warned longer term challenges remained for the tourism and hospitality sector.
"I've seen tourism decline the entire time that I've been doing this in the past 20 years," he said.
Visit Guernsey's marketing manager Sam Claxton said there had been some "uplift" in visitor numbers "which may be linked to the recent heatwave".
Claxton said the accommodation occupancy rate in Guernsey had reached 84% in June, up from 79% in June 2025 and 2024.
Airport passenger numbers were up by 3% in June and 10% in July compared with the same months last year and the number of ferry passengers in July was up by 8% compared with July 2025, he added.
Andy Furniss, who runs Le Petit Train trips in St Peter Port, said German, Dutch and French visitors day trippers from St Malo have been "incredible for trade".
Furniss said: "Our trade this year is significantly up on last year, even with a 60% decline in cruise ships coming to Guernsey.
"Walk-up trade is significantly higher this year than it has been since 2019."

articles.title: UK weather: Significant drop in temperatures this weekend as heatwave ends - BBC
articles.search_term: (heatwave OR "heat wave" OR "severe heatwave" OR "extreme heat" OR "heat spell" OR "scorching heat" OR "blistering heat" OR "sweltering heat" OR "hot winds" OR loo OR "hot loo winds" OR "intense heat" OR "unbearable heat" OR "deadly heat" OR heat OR "weather forecast" OR "weather update" OR "weather alert" OR "IMD forecast" OR "IMD prediction" OR "IMD alert" OR IMD OR "rising temperatures" OR "temperatures expected to rise" OR "relief from heat" OR "respite from heat" OR "heat respite" OR "respite from scorching heat") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
articles.full_text:
- Published
Temperatures are set to tumble this weekend as the fifth heatwave to scorch the UK this year comes to an end.
After Thursday marked the hottest day of 2026 so far, conditions will be noticeably cooler on Saturday and Sunday.
Temperatures will fall by 10-15 degrees Celsius by the end of the weekend, bringing them much closer to the seasonal average.
The change in weather pattern that is bringing this cooler air will also result in an increased chance of rain, including in areas currently in drought.
Friday became the 39th day this year in which somewhere in the UK hit 30C (86F) or higher as the latest bout of extreme heat clung on in southern areas.
This smashed the previous UK record of 30 days set in 1995.
It was also only the ninth time since records began where a temperature of 37C (99F) or more has been registered.
Three of those occasions have been in 2026, sending a clear message that our climate is changing rapidly.
Dramatic drop in temperatures across the UK
The impact of the heat has been seen and felt in most aspects of daily life, from raging wildfires and transport delays to an increase in heat-related deaths, and for many the cooldown will be welcomed.
The change is being brought about by a cold front that has been moving south-eastwards through Friday and Friday night, introducing winds from a cooler north-westerly direction, as well as bringing a few showers.
While a few spots in south-east England could still reach their heatwave temperature threshold values of 27 or 28 Celsius on Saturday, many areas will be 10-13 degrees Celsius cooler than on Thursday.
Much of the UK, away from the south-east, will see highs of 16-24C.
These values are around average for mid-August but, given the exceptional heat experienced by many areas so far this summer, may feel comparatively cool.
Most areas will be dry with sunny spells, although a few showers are likely in north-west Scotland and East Anglia.
Will there be more heatwaves this summer?
Most forecasts show that the cooler and more changeable spell of weather is set to continue for the rest of the month.
Some forecasts are also hinting at the potential for more significant rain-bearing low pressure systems tracking closer to the UK.
Temperatures are therefore more likely to stay closer to the seasonal average.
Some spells of warmer cannot be ruled out, especially in the south, but it looks unlikely at this time that further heatwaves will build this month.
While the meteorological summer comes to a close at the end of August it is not unusual for the UK for experience bouts of heat in September.

How we can all help prevent wildfires?
More than two weeks after a devastating wildfire whipped through two Suffolk coastal nature reserves, similar fires broke out elsewhere in England and Wales.
Tinder-dry conditions caused by weeks and weeks with little rain have resulted in the ideal conditions for flames to take hold.
Not only have much-loved landscapes and rare habitats been damaged, but homes and businesses were put at risk, and the emergency services were put under strain.
So, what can we all do to help prevent their spread?
How many wildfires have taken place this year?
Firefighters have responded to 966 wildfires across England and Wales this year, including 185 in the first 10 days of August alone, according to the National Fire Chiefs Council.
The figure for 2026 included a blaze at a 660-acre (270 hectares) peatland nature reserve at Holme Fen, near Peterborough, and a wildfire at Kenninghall, near Diss, Norfolk, which spread to nearby homes, causing serious damage.
Firefighters were also tackling an "unpredictable" fire affecting an area the size of about 230 football pitches in the New Forest, Hampshire, which started on Sunday.
What conditions are needed?
Of course, dry weather does not, on its own, cause wildfires - there needs to be a source of ignition too, such as a spark from a barbecue or a discarded cigarette.
However, dry conditions remove moisture from vegetation, making it more able to burn and act as fuel for blazes to take hold and spread.
The conditions the UK is experiencing so far this summer, in its fifth heatwave of the year, mirror the warnings given by climate scientists that human-induced climate change would lead to more frequent and intense heatwaves, as well as potential summer droughts.
What can the public do to help?
Suffolk's chief fire officer Jon Lacey has urged the public to "remain vigilant" and avoid having barbecues, bonfires or throwing cigarettes on the ground.
The fire service advice includes:
- Avoid lighting barbecues and campfires near vegetation such as grass, heathland or woodland - only use them in designated safe areas
- Leave no trace - take all litter home or dispose of it in bins provided
- Ensure cigarettes and smoking materials are fully extinguished and disposed of responsibly
- Douse disposable barbecues with water, allow them to cool completely, then dispose of them in household (black) bins - never in public bins
Hampshire & Isle of Wight Fire & Rescue Service urged people to "pack a picnic instead of a barbecue".
People also need to think about the safe disposal of vapes.
Sam Kench, Suffolk's Wildlife Wise delivery manager, said: "As the weather gets warmer, we want people to enjoy spending time outdoors, but we are asking visitors not to bring sources of fire to our wildlife sites.
"While many people are aware that cigarettes are a common cause of outdoor fires, fewer realise they also contribute to plastic pollution, posing a dual risk to wildlife.
"Similarly, disposable vapes - which are becoming increasingly common - can ignite if exposed to extreme temperatures."
He urged users to take them to dedicated recycling points.
What about barbeques at home?
Plenty of families want to enjoy garden gatherings around a barbecue.
Essex Fire and Rescue Service has issued advice on how to do so safely.
- Always place barbecues on a non-flammable and even surface
- Make sure it is well away from houses, sheds and fences or anything else that could catch fire
- Follow the safety instructions
- Never put hot ashes straight into a dustbin or wheelie bin - they could melt the plastic and cause a fire
- After cooking, turn the gas supply off first, and then the barbecue control. This will stop any gas from leaking
What should farmers do if a wildfire starts?
"One of our biggest risks during these spells of hot weather is fires on rural farmland," said Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue group commander James Balls.
"Farm fires can result in the loss of machinery, livestock, stores of hay and straw, and the destruction of buildings; a serious fire on a farm can affect the financial stability of even the most well-run business."
The fire service's advice for farmers included:
- Download the What3words app to give a precise location to emergency services
- Ensure your farm is clearly signposted and make sure you keep all access routes clear in case emergency vehicles need to access the site
- Make sure everyone on the farm knows the fire plan
- Keep any firefighting equipment easily accessible and ensure everyone knows where it's stored
- Make sure you have an animal evacuation plan for your livestock in the event of a fire
'Waiting for rain'
At their height, the fires at Holme Fen, Dunwich Heath and in the New Forest have been supported by crews from other parts of the country.
Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue's area commander, Wayne Swales, said: "We're one service in isolation - if you look at the wildfires going on across the country, all services are pulling on those same resources, which makes it even tougher."
"Summer is usually the busiest time of year for us, but the summer season hasn't been the standard two weeks in July. We've been like this since June, so we are, like everyone, waiting for rain."

Temporary ban on disposable BBQs as military deployed to help battle wildfires
Disposable barbecues have been temporarily banned from sale over fears they pose a "significant risk to the public" as drought and heatwave conditions continue to grip the UK.
They have been the cause of "a number of serious wildfires across the country over the summer months", the government said.
A potential ban was first discussed at an emergency Cobra meeting in response to record temperatures earlier this week. The public have been urged not to light an open fires and to dispose of cigarettes carefully.
Meanwhile Prime Minister Andy Burnham says the country is like "a tinderbox", as 200 personnel have now been deployed to help emergency teams tackling wildfires around the country.
As part of the military deployment, Gurkha logistics teams equipped with water tankers and military engineers are now assisting fire services in South Wales.
Andy Burnham has promised more military personnel will be deployed elsewhere if needed.
Crews in England and Wales tackled multiple blazes on Friday and an emergency alert was sent to millions of phones.
A total of 1,017 wildfires have been recorded in England and Wales this year, according to data shared by the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC), which matches last year's record.
On Friday evening, an emergency alert was sent to mobile phones warning of a "very high risk of wildfires nationally" across England and Wales.
The message asked residents, landowners and visitors to not undertake any activity that could cause a fire "including disposable barbecues, firepits, garden incinerators of fireworks".
It was the most extensive use of the system to date, according to the government.
Disposable barbecues "cannot be considered a safe product" in the current conditions and they "must not be made available for sale either in store or online at the current time" in Great Britain, according to the advice published by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (DBIST).
The ban applies to England, Scotland and Wales, but not Northern Ireland.
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the measures were "common-sense steps to protect lives and the environment."
All retailers will be receiving guidance about the change, which will be kept under review, Burnham told the BBC.
He also said some of the wildfires burning across the country will have been started by disposable barbecues.
Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live's Matt Chorley, the prime minister said: "We've got 37 fires across England and Wales right now, four of them are major incidents."
He added: "We're going into a difficult weekend, please just think about the situation that we're in.
"Britain is a tinderbox right now. Setting a fire in any outdoor setting of any kind is a risk to other people's homes, it's a risk to other people's lives, don't do it, please don't do it."
It said that retailers should suspend sales once an extreme heat event has been declared as imminent, or in response to "reasonable, evidence based" requests from local councils.
He told the BBC: "We know the risks that disposable barbecues have been causing and to have a ban on them is much-needed, much-called-for and I hope it becomes long-term."
Burnham also said he planned to commission firefighting planes, like those used in Europe and the US, to combat the spread of wildfires.
He said plans were being drawn up for emergency financial support for fire services battling the spread of wildfires.
"We have a fire and rescue service across the country that isn't properly set up to deal with these incidents," Burnham said.
"We don't have the capability in the way that we should have to fight these fires.
"There's thousands of firefighters out there today doing back-breaking work, in full kit, in the most difficult conditions", he added.
He said the UK must face up to the "changing climate" and transition to "more clean energy".
His comments came ahead of the appointment of Baroness Blake of Leeds as fire minister.
Friends of the Earth urged the prime minister to tackle the "root cause" of the "climate emergency" that is fuelling this summer's extreme weather events.
"Without urgent action to curb the carbon emissions driving this crisis, future heatwaves, droughts and wildfires will only get worse and the ability for future generations to adapt will disappear" the environmental group warned.
Burnham was speaking during a visit to Stourbridge to see the impact of a devastating blaze.
As the UK experienced its hottest day of the year on Thursday, residents fled their homes when fires spread through dry grass and tore through houses.
West Midlands Ambulance Service said it treated 54 casualties at eight different fires across the region. Nineteen people were taken to hospital for treatment.
In 2025, fire and rescue services in England and Wales broke a new record when they responded to nearly 1,000 wildfire incidents, with the NFCC warning at the time that climate change is increasing their risk and severity.
The conditions the UK is experiencing so far this summer also mirror the warnings given by climate scientists that human-induced climate change would lead to more frequent and intense heatwaves, as well as potential summer droughts.

articles.full_text:
A lot has gone wrong for Honda this year: factory riders Jake Dixon and Somkiat Chantra have missed numerous races due to injury, and despite an extensive development programme behind the scenes centred on record champion Jonathan Rea, the Fireblade is proving even weaker than in previous years. The crushing reality: whilst Ducati has already clinched the Constructors’ World Championship with four rounds to spare and leads the standings at the summer break with 496 points – the maximum! – the Honda riders have scraped together a paltry 20 points. This leaves the world’s largest motorbike manufacturer languishing in last place – 90 points behind the team in second-last place.
Honda is certainly not lacking in commitment: whilst Dixon and Chantra were fine-tuning their set-up on Thursday and Friday (13–14 August) at the Circuit de Nevers Magny-Cours, the test team featuring Rea was in action elsewhere. For the two regular riders, the test was valuable not only from a development perspective: neither was familiar with the circuit in central France, so it also served as good preparation for the first event after the summer break, taking place there on the first weekend of September.
With track temperatures reaching 65 (!) degrees Celsius, Dixon and Chantra completed 69 and 103 laps on Thursday, and 70 and 94 on Friday. Whilst the main focus on the first day was on the basic set-up of the CBR1000RR-R, work on the second day centred on the suspension, the electronics and comparing different set-ups. The data collected will serve as the basis for the next test on 25–26 August at Estoril, near Lisbon.
New territory for both Honda riders
“I like the track at Magny-Cours,” said Dixon. “It’s a bit tricky to get to grips with, but it’s a lovely track. It was very hot. Ultimately, it was just a test – there are no prizes to be won – so we focused on working through the test plan prepared by the team and gathering as much information as possible. We had a lot to do, but I’m satisfied.”
The Thai rider Chantra added: “As it was my first time riding at Magny-Cours, I was able to spend a lot of time getting to know the circuit whilst also working on the bike. We were able to gather a lot of useful information. That’s important because during a race weekend we don’t have as much time to try out different solutions, whereas now we were able to focus on this sort of work. I was able to improve my lap time from session to session; on the first day, I set my fastest time in the afternoon, which was very positive.”
Honda did not release any lap times, nor did the other participants. Alongside Honda, the BMW works team was present with its regular riders Miguel Oliveira and Danilo Petrucci, as well as test rider Michael van der Mark; the Marc VDS privateer Ducati team, featuring Sam Lowes, was also in attendance.

JEFFERSON, LA – The National Weather Service has issued an Extreme Heat Warning for all of Jefferson Parish tomorrow (Saturday, Aug. 15, 2026) from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m., and an Extreme Heat Watch for Sunday from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. Actual temperatures will reach the mid-to-upper 90s. Humidity values will increase this weekend, leading to heat index values from 110 to 115 degrees.
Due to the extreme heat, the Jefferson Parish Library’s East Bank Regional and West Bank Regional branches will be open from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Saturday and Sunday. Residents are welcome to utilize these facilities to stay cool. All other Library branches will follow regular hours; for locations and hours, visit www.JPLibrary.net. Residents in need of assistance can contact the Jefferson Parish Emergency Operations Center at (504) 349-5360.
Consecutive days of dangerous heat can take a serious toll on a person’s body. The public should remain weather aware and take precautionary measures to avoid becoming a victim of heat exhaustion and related illnesses. Heat-related illnesses, like heat exhaustion or heat stroke, happen when the body is not able to properly cool itself. While the body normally cools itself by sweating, during extreme heat, this might not be enough. In these cases, a person’s body temperature rises faster than it can cool itself down. This can cause damage to the brain and other vital organs. Some factors that might increase your risk of developing a heat-related illness include high levels of humidity, obesity, fever, dehydration, prescription drug use, heart disease, mental illness, poor circulation, sunburn and alcohol use.
Heat-related illnesses and deaths are preventable:
- Wear lightweight, light-colored, loose-fitting clothing
- Stay indoors in air conditioning and limiting outdoor activities
- Look before you lock your car. The fastest heating rate inside a car occurs in the first 30 minutes. Never leave people or pets alone in a closed car.
During high temperatures, it is important to monitor those at high risk, including infants and young children, people 65 or older, those who are overweight, people who overexert during work or exercise and people who are physically ill (especially with heart disease or high blood pressure), or who take certain medications, such as for depression, insomnia or poor circulation.
It is also important to protect your four-legged friends during hot weather months. Jefferson Protection & Animal Welfare Services recommends the following:
- Animals’ paws are just as tender as your feet, so please check the pavement with your hand; if it’s too hot for you, it’s too hot for them. Pet shoes or booties help keep their paws safe.
- Even though you and your pets need exercise, it is important to avoid going out during the hottest part of the day.
- Much like humans, animals can also get sunburned; monitor your pet for burns (short and light-colored fur). Apply animal-safe sunblock, if necessary.
- A pet’s fur may actually help keep them cool in the hotter months, so reconsider before cutting off all their fur, but keep them properly groomed.
- Some pets may be more susceptible to heat (Bulldogs, Pugs, etc.); monitor these breeds for breathing issues.
- Bring water when going on a long walk, even in the earliest or latest part of the day.
- DO NOT leave your pet in a hot vehicle.
For more information about Jefferson Parish, visit www.JeffParish.gov. Residents can also receive regular updates by following the Parish on social media (@JeffParishGov) or by texting JPALERT (for English) or JPNOTICIAS (for Spanish) to 888-777.

articles.full_text:
Extremely dry weather has hit much of the country, with more than 70% of the country now in drought following a record dry July, and an August that has so far seen just 5% of expected rainfall.
Thursday was also the fifth hottest day on record in the UK, and further records were set, according to the Met Office.
This is now the first year on record to see three separate days where temperatures reached the 37C threshold, as well as the first year with four days at 36C or above.
Friday is also expected to be a scorching day, with highs of 33C predicted in the capital.
Temperatures are then due to fall to the mid 20s over the weekend, giving a welcome respite from the extreme heat for many.
The UK is facing increasingly extreme conditions such as heatwaves, drought and wildfires fuelled by climate change, which is mostly driven by greenhouse gas emissions from burning fossil fuels for power plants, vehicles, heating and industry.
Baroness Brown, who chairs the independent advisory Climate Change Committee’s adaptation work, warned it “gets worse from here” until greenhouse gas emissions are cut to zero overall, known as net zero.
Climate advisers are also urging the Government to take steps to prepare the UK for worsening extremes, from making it easier for farmers to build reservoirs to putting air conditioning in hospitals and providing grants for vulnerable families to do the same.
England and Wales have already seen as many wildfires this year as during the whole of 2025.
Some 1,017 wildfires have been recorded in England and Wales this year, according to data shared by the National Fire Chiefs Council, the same as last year’s record-breaking total.

Balasore (Odisha) [India], August 15 (ANI): Fresh flooding triggered by heavy rainfall has affected several districts of Odisha, with Balasore among the worst-hit areas, prompting the administration to intensify relief and rescue measures.
According to officials, Balasore, Mayurbhanj, Bhadrak, Jajpur, Sundargarh and Keonjhar have been affected by the latest spell of flooding. Floodwater has affected hundreds of villages across the districts, with authorities evacuating more than 41,000 people to safer locations as a precautionary measure.
In Balasore, Remuna block, Balasore Sadar block and parts of Bahanaga and Basta have been affected by the floods.
Speaking about the situation, Balasore District Magistrate Suryavanshi Mayur Vikas said the administration has deployed officials across the affected areas and is closely monitoring developments.
'Remuna block, Balasore Sadar block, and some areas of Bahanaga and Basta have been affected by floods. It is raining in Jharkhand, so there is a high possibility of water coming from there as well. All officials have been deployed in the area,' the District Magistrate said.
He said the administration's immediate focus was to ensure that essential supplies reached people affected by the flooding.
'We are trying to ensure that food and drinking water reach all people affected by the floods. Medical teams have also been put on alert,' Vikas said.
The administration is particularly keeping a watch on the possibility of additional water entering northern Odisha following rainfall in neighbouring Jharkhand.
The fresh spell of flooding has come after two days of heavy rainfall, which has caused rivers in northern Odisha to swell and inundate villages and roads in several districts. Authorities have opened relief centres and moved people from low-lying areas to safer locations.
According to reports, 429 villages across 52 blocks in the affected districts have been impacted by floodwater. Rescue and relief operations have been stepped up, with 79 rescue teams deployed in the affected areas.
In Balasore, several areas have reported waterlogging and inundation following heavy rainfall. The administration has been monitoring vulnerable locations and making arrangements for evacuation wherever required.
The latest flood situation has also raised concerns in neighbouring Mayurbhanj and Bhadrak, along with Jajpur, Sundargarh and Keonjhar. Authorities are monitoring river levels and rainfall in these districts and have kept disaster-response teams ready.
The Central Water Commission has also warned of a flash-flood risk in parts of Odisha, while the India Meteorological Department has forecast further heavy rainfall in several parts of the state. An alert was issued for 11 districts amid continuing rainfall activity.
Authorities are therefore maintaining heightened vigilance in vulnerable areas and coordinating evacuation, relief distribution and medical preparedness. (ANI)

EMSA's Medical Heat Alert for Tulsa still in effect
TULSA, Okla. — With scorching temperatures continuing to impact the Tulsa area, EMSA said its Medical Heat Alert for Tulsa remains in effect.
On Wednesday, EMSA reported they had responded to 50 heat-related illness calls and transported 33 people to the hospital for further treatment.
EMSA said it has continued to respond to heat-related illness calls over the past few days, including five calls on Wednesday with two patients taken to the hospital and seven calls on Thursday with four patients taken to the hospital.
As extreme temperatures continue, EMSA is asking the public to take all possible precautions to stay safe in the heat.
Listed below are some heat safety tips provided by EMSA:
- "Hydrate before you need it. Drink plenty of water and electrolyte-replacement beverages several hours before and during prolonged outdoor activity.
- Wear lightweight, loose-fitting, light-colored clothing and a wide-brimmed hat when outdoors.
- Take frequent breaks in shaded or air-conditioned areas.
- Avoid alcohol and limit caffeine intake, as both can contribute to dehydration.
- If you do not have air conditioning, visit a cooling center or public indoor space such as a library, community center or shopping mall.
- Use air conditioning whenever possible during extreme heat.
- Work outdoors with a partner and check on elderly neighbors, friends and family members.
- Carry a cell phone when spending time outdoors so help can be summoned quickly if symptoms develop."
This is currently the third Medical Heat Alert issued by EMSA in 2026.
